p.d: निम्नलिखित गद्यांश को पढ़कर प्रश्नों के उत्तर दीजिए।
p.b:
Freedom is never a gift that is graciously handed down; it is earned by those who refuse to accept an unjust order. History shows that every advance in human liberty was bought with the labour and often the blood of ordinary people. The authorities have rarely surrendered power willingly. When a people begin to question an established arrangement, the first response of those in command is seldom argument. They reach instead for the instruments of control — the denial of assembly, the silencing of printers, the arrest of speakers. Yet no such measure has ever lasted, because a demand once voiced cannot be unheard.

Real freedom, however, is not merely the absence of interference. A person released from outward restraint but bound inwardly by fear, greed or habit is not free in any meaningful sense. The author therefore distinguishes between two conditions: the freedom of the body, which laws can grant, and the freedom of the mind, which no law can confer. Only the second permits a human being to choose deliberately rather than react. Endeavours directed towards the first without the second produce a citizen who is technically unchained yet practically obedient.

p.d: निम्नलिखित गद्यांश को पढ़कर प्रश्नों के उत्तर दीजिए।
p.b:
The Himalayan state of Uttarakhand is often described as the water tower of northern India, and the description is not merely poetic. From its glaciers issue the Ganga, the Yamuna and a dozen lesser rivers that between them sustain the plains of half a subcontinent. The bounty of the mountains is thus felt far beyond the mountains themselves, in fields that their farmers will never see.

What is less often recognised is that this bounty depends on a benevolent climate that is no longer dependable. Receding snow-lines, erratic monsoons and the sudden bursting of glacial lakes have altered a balance that held for centuries. The springs that once ran through the dry months now fail. Villages that stood on ridges for the sake of defence must now be abandoned for want of water.

It follows that water should be central to our thinking about this region, and not treated as one concern among many. Every road cut into a slope, every hotel raised above a spring line, changes the movement of water that millions depend upon downstream. The mountains ask very little of us. They ask only that we understand what we are taking.

1. There is something we all want to do, although few of us readily admit it: Get rid of guests.

2. For nine months in the year, only my closest friends come to see me. Then, when temperatures start soaring in the plains, long-lost acquaintances suddenly remember that I exist, and people whom I am barely able to recognize appear at the front door, willing to have me put them up for periods ranging from six days to six weeks.

3. Occasionally, I am the master of the situation. I inform them that the cottage is already bursting, that people are sleeping on the floor. If the hopefuls start looking around for signs of these uncomfortable guests, I remark that they have all gone out for a picnic.

4. The other day I received visitors who proved to be more thick-skinned than most. The man was a friend of a friend of an acquaintance of mine. I had never seen him before. But on the strength of this distant relationship, he had brought his family along.

5. I tried the usual ploy but it didn't work. The man and his family were perfectly willing to share the floor with any others who might be staying with me.

6. So I made my next move. 'I must warn you about the scorpions', I said. The scorpion-scare is effective with most people. But I was dealing with professionals. The man set his son rolling up the carpet. 'Sometimes centipedes fall from the ceiling', I said desperately.

7. We were now interrupted by someone knocking on the front door. It was the postman with a rejected manuscript, his arrival inspired me to greater inventiveness.

8. 'I'm terribly sorry', I said, staring hard at a rejection slip. 'I'm afraid I have to leave immediately. A paper wants me to interview the Maharishi. I hope you won't mind. Would you like the name of a good hotel?'

9. 'Oh, don't worry about us', said the woman expansively. 'We'll look after the house while you are away.'

1. The study of handwriting is known as graphology and it has been practised for hundreds of years. Professional forensic graphologists have worked on many court cases to use handwriting to link suspects with crimes.

2. Handwriting is particularly important legally in the case of signatures and proving whether signatures are real or forged can be pivotal. Graphologists also work to verify whether autographs are real or fake.

3. Some handwriting analysts also study writing samples to determine personality types and some businesses commission this analysis before hiring new employees. The method is even sometimes used to help couples see if they are compatible. According to graphologists, there is very little you can't tell from a persons' handwriting.

4. From psychological conditions like high blood pressure and schizophrenia to personality traits like dominance and aggression: if you write by hand, graphologists can analyse you.

5. Everything from the size of your letters to how closely you space words can reveal intricate details of your personality. In general, the size of your letters can reveal whether you are shy or outgoing. Compared to a standard lined sheet of paper, if you write with tiny letters that do not reach the top line, you are likely to have a timid and introverted personality. If you write with large letters that go over the topline, you are likely to be opposite: outgoing, confident and attention seeking.

6. Studies suggest that people who space words widely like freedom and independence, whereas those choosing to write with small spaces prefer to be among others and do not like to be alone.

p.b: At least a third of the ice in the Himalayas and the Hindu Kush region will melt this century as temperatures rise, disrupting river flows vital for growing crops from China to India, according to the scientists. Vast glacial reserves that feed rivers like the Indus, Ganges and Brahmaputra are receding rapidly.

p.d: निम्नलिखित गद्यांश को पढ़कर प्रश्नों के उत्तर दीजिए।
p.b: Heaven seems to turn up when we least expect it. I gave up a good job in Delhi and came to live in a hill station; partly because I love mountains and forests and partly because I wanted to devote more time to writing. I live at the edge of a forest of oak and maple. I am happy among trees but the full magic of a tree was only brought home to me some time ago when I was in the plains.

Meera had grown up believing that her father's work was the most important job on the coast. Every evening, when the sun sank behind the headland, he climbed the one hundred and twelve steps of the lighthouse tower, trimmed the wick, and set the great lamp turning. A single beam swept across the dark water, and ships a long way out adjusted their course towards safety.

It was not an easy life. In the monsoon the wind tore at the shutters and the sea threw spray as high as the gallery rail. Twice the supply boat failed to come for a whole month, and the family lived on rice, dried fish and whatever grew in the small garden behind the keeper's cottage. Meera learned to repair the lamp mechanism when she was fourteen, because her father's hands had begun to shake and he could no longer hold the fine tools steady.

When the government decided to automate the light, an engineer arrived with crates of instruments and stayed for three weeks. He was polite, and he explained everything carefully, but Meera noticed that he never once climbed to the lamp room at night. The new system was reliable, he said. It would never need trimming.

The night the light was switched over, Meera stood on the gallery and watched the automatic beam turn. It was steadier than her father's had ever been. There was no flicker, no moment when the flame guttered in a sudden draught. It was, she admitted to herself, better.

Two winters later a fishing boat came ashore in a storm. Its engine had failed and the crew had been guided in by the beam. The captain climbed up to thank them, and when he saw Meera's father sitting in the doorway with his hands wrapped around a cup of tea, he asked him how long he had kept the light. Forty years, her father said. The captain looked at the automatic lamp and then back at the old man, and said that he had never once thought about who was up there. He had only ever trusted that someone was.

The moment the train halted, 'Chhutti' would appear - a brown dog with pointed ears and a wagging tail. The platform people lovingly called him 'Porter No. 22'. Ramu, the sweeper, said the dog would run ahead of every train as if clearing the platform. One afternoon, a bull that had slipped off its chain stormed onto the crowded platform. Everyone ran helter-skelter. Chhutti barked and circled the bull until the gardeners quietly led it out. In appreciation, everyone fed him warm jalebis. That evening Chhutti taught us a lesson - courage lives not in size but in the heart.

Walk upon the road of truth, hold the hand of right,

However hard the turns may be, never lose the sight.

Small the house of falsehood, soon it tumbles down,

High the wall of truth stands - it wears a shining crown.
